title: Gender differentiated livelihood vulnerability to climate change and variability: Experience of rural households in northern Ethiopia
content:
by Fentahun Gebrie Mucha, Zerihun Yohannes Amare, Solomon Addisu Legesse

Climate change disproportionately affects economically and socially disadvantaged groups, where differences in livelihood vulnerability frequently intensified by gender inequalities, although empirical evidence remains limited. The vulnerability of rural households’ livelihoods to climate change is influenced by socioeconomic and biophysical contexts; however, the assessment of gendered vulnerability remains limited in northern Ethiopia. This study aimed to examine rural households’ livelihood vulnerability to climate change and variability through a gender lens. Employing a mixed research approach with a concurrent design, data collection was carried out through household surveys, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations. A multistage sampling technique was employed to choose the sample households, and the Livelihood Vulnerability Index based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (LVI-IPCC) framework, which assesses vulnerability through exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity, was used to analyze of livelihood vulnerability. Data were collected from 396 surveyed households, six focus group discussions and nine key informants. The findings from the LVI-IPCC indicate a statistically significant gender difference in livelihood vulnerability. Female-headed households (FHHs) show higher vulnerability (0.098) compared to male-headed households (MHHs) (0.061), primarily attributed to higher sensitivity (0.550) and lower adaptive capacity (0.380). However, MHHs show lower sensitivity (0.507) and greater adaptive capacity (0.491). Nevertheless, no significant gender difference was found in the exposure component. These findings underline the necessity for targeted and gender-transformative interventions to strengthen the adaptive capacity of FHHs by improving access to agricultural technologies, climate information services, skill development, livelihood diversification opportunities, and financial services, including inclusive microfinance.
